face: South gullies to the Eye Col, then the summit block above it
overview: East Twin Needle (7,868 ft) is the eastern and slightly lower of the Twin Needles pinnacles in the Southern Pickets, 0.55 mi west of Mount Terror and just east of its taller sister summit, West Twin Needle (7,936 ft). William Degenhardt, James Martin, and Herb Strandberg made the first ascent of West Twin Needle on August 17, 1932. East Twin Needle was not climbed on that trip, and its first ascent came later. Composed of solid Skagit gneiss, the pair rises above Crescent Creek Basin near the Mu
beta: The South Route climbs East Twin Needle from Crescent Creek Basin by the loose south-facing gullies to the Eye Col (about 7,400 ft), the notch between East and West Twin Needle. Small chockstones low in the gully are scrambled past; the larger ones higher up are fifth class and are usually pitched, and a short scree walk finishes at the col. From the col the route climbs the steep summit block directly above, with a short hand-crack crux near the top that can hold ice early in the season; the su

first_pass.evidence: Only online description of the south side is the AAJ descent: downclimb/rap to Eye Col, then fourth-class gullies with raps; no grade found for the summit block above Eye Col, record's 5.7 kept.

fa: Ed Cooper and Stuart Ferguson — September 15, 1961
overview: A steep face of rock and ice on the northeast side of Forbidden Peak: rock below and above a single steep ice patch (about 50°) in the middle of the face. Best in firm early-season conditions, it is a rarely climbed line in a shaded, remote North Cascades cirque.
breakdown: Lower face: Rock, a few pitons

first_pass.evidence: AAJ FA account: 300 ft of rock, then a 300-ft 50-degree ice patch, then easier upslab rock; no modern grade found.
first_pass.note: Headline "IV" with grade_system yds is not a difficulty grade. 50-degree ice is about AI2 (record says AI3). Rock difficulty unstated (old "grade III" wording, a few pitons); if the rock proves 5th class, re-grade on yds.

overview: A steeper, more technical alternative on Fortress's northeast-facing side: several pitches of rock up a headwall, followed by a long snow slope studded with rock islands. The route tops out on the ridge crest short of the true summit, requiring further ridge travel to finish.
beta: Very little beta exists online for this line beyond a single forum report: it follows the left side of the visible northeast face, with steeper rock and snow options further right of uncertain quality/rock condition. Expect a mixed rock-and-snow outing rather than a simple scramble, with a rope needed for the pitched rock section. One climber who used it noted that the published descriptions of it are inaccurate.

first_pass.evidence: Only the ridge toward the Chiwawa saddle is described online (4th-class chimney); no source for the NE headwall pitches.

face: Southeast ridge/face of the summit block
fa: Ed Cooper, Glen Denny, Joan Firey, Joe Firey, and George Whitmore, September 10, 1961 (first ascent of the peak)
overview: Frenzel Spitz (7,440 ft) is the smallest and most remote of the three-summit Crescent Creek Spires cluster in the Southern Pickets, tucked directly beneath the north face of Ottohorn on the ridge connecting the Southern and Northern Pickets. Because it sits off the main crest and is only reachable by crossing the Ottohorn–Himmelhorn col and descending about 500 ft below Ottohorn's north face, it is one of the more inaccessible technical summits in the North Cascades — it wasn't climbed until Sep
beta: Frenzel Spitz sits off the main Pickets crest between the Northern and Southern subranges, close under Ottohorn's north face; the 1961 first-ascent party reached it by descending roughly 500 feet from Ottohorn after climbing that peak the same day. It is rarely climbed in isolation — most parties link it with Himmelhorn, Ottohorn, and/or other Crescent Creek Basin objectives given the difficulty of getting there at all.

first_pass.evidence: No route-specific source found online; kept the record's 5.6.
first_pass.note: Record headline says Grade III while commitment says II; could not resolve.

rock_grade: Class 4 scrambling on the standard line; a short 5.4 pitch on Beckey's optional 'Chimney Variation'
fa: Jim Crooks and Judson Nelson, August 27, 1940 (a fixed ring piton attributed to this ascent remains in #2 Gully)
overview: Garfield Mountain is a rugged granodiorite massif of five named summits (Main/East Peak 5,519 ft, West Peak 4,896 ft, North Peak 5,101 ft, plus the Leaning Spire) rising more than 4,400 ft above the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River in barely a mile — one of the steepest, most relief-dense peaks in the western Cascades. Despite a local reputation as a 'scramble,' every summit actually requires roped technical climbing: documented lines range from the 5.3 Southwest Ledges to the 23-pitch 5.10c sport r
beta: From the Taylor River trailhead, a cross-country line follows a dry creek bed, then a brushy, flagged climbers' path through the 'dirt gully,' a soloable 2-pitch slab, a traverse under a rock outcrop, the 'Razorback,' 'Glade Saddle' (a tight 2-person bivy site), a 'wooded ramp,' the roped 'Key Ledge Traverse,' the 'Y Notch' (head of 'The Great Canyon'), and finally '#2 Gully' — loose rock on one side, polished/mossy on the other — which gains the upper mountain via a mix of simul-climbing and be

first_pass.evidence: Trip report on the south route: mostly class 2-3, with two easy class-5 leads on the chimney variation.

face: South side of the Main Peak — dirt gully, slab, Key Ledge and #2 Gully to the summit
fa: Jim Crooks & Judson Nelson, August 27, 1940 (first ascent of Garfield Mountain; a fixed ring piton in #2 Gully is believed to be theirs)
overview: The standard line to Garfield's true 5,519 ft summit and the one Beckey called 'a hazardous enigma': 4,400 feet of dirt gully, brush, slab and ledge navigation from the Middle Fork road to the Y Notch, then four or five pitches of loose, barely protectable low-5th climbing up #2 Gully to the summit slabs. Under two miles horizontally and a minimum of twelve hours.
beta: The old sketch landmarks are still the way people navigate it: dirt gully, slab, canyon edge, tiny notch, razorback, glade saddle, key ledge traverse, Y notch, #2 gully. Walk up the dry creek bed from the road; partway up the route leaves the streambed into the woods on faint trail and flagging. At about 2,200 ft you reach the dirt gully — fill water at the creek here, it is the last certain water on the route. Four hundred vertical feet of loose dirt and rock, then the trail exits left into bru
breakdown: S4 — outcrop, razorback, tiny notch: Class 3
S6 — Key Ledge Traverse to the Y Notch: Class 3-4
S9 — summit slabs and heather: Class 3-4 with a low-5th move

first_pass.evidence: Described as easy/low 5th class (several loose pitches); no published number found, kept the record's 5.4.

face: South and west sides of the peak (route avoids the peak's much steeper east face)
fa: Carla Firey, Joan Firey, David Knudson, Peter Renz — July 17, 1970 (during the 11-day 'Carpetbaggers Traverse' of the Goodell Creek drainage)
overview: Ghost Peak is a Northern Pickets summit near Crooked Thumb and Challenger, completing the spectral naming theme of the range. Its infrequent ascents make it a quiet objective for those deep in the Pickets.
beta: Ghost Peak is normally climbed as an add-on from a high camp shared with neighboring Crooked Thumb Peak and Phantom Peak, since all three summits are within a few tenths of a mile of one another in the Northern Pickets. The way from camp is obvious once you're established there. The first-ascent party climbed from the notch south of the peak, reaching it from the west, then kept to the south and west sides of the mountain along obvious weaknesses — easy-to-moderate 4th/low-5th-class climbing on

first_pass.evidence: Easiest route listed as Class 4 (West Face); FA account quoted by the record (easy-moderate fifth class) not found online.
first_pass.note: Headline is "Class 4" but grade_system is yds and rock_grade says 5th class; internally inconsistent.

ice_grade: Low-angle alpine ice (roughly AI1) on the upper headwall when icy; otherwise steep snow
overview: The Kennedy Glacier ascends Glacier Peak's northwest flank and offers a more glaciated, slightly steeper alternative to the standard routes. It is a popular ski-mountaineering descent and a fine summer climb when crevasses are well bridged.
beta: From a camp near Glacier Creek, follow a climbers' trail up a gully to the top of Kennedy Ridge, then descend (right) to the foot of the Kennedy Glacier. Ascend the lower glacier keeping right, then the center of the upper glacier. Approach the bergschrund at the head of the glacier by ascending left to the top of a snow dome, find a snow bridge to cross it, then climb the center of a roughly 40° headwall, staying left of but close to prominent rock outcrops, to the crater rim.
breakdown: Kennedy Ridge to foot of glacier: Climbers' trail, easy snow
Lower to upper Kennedy Glacier: Glacier, deeply crevassed
Crater and summit slope: ~45° snow, often icy

first_pass.evidence: Upper headwall ~40-45 degree snow, often icy (about 180 ft); no ice grade published for the Kennedy route.
first_pass.note: Mapped steep, often-icy snow with no published ice grade to Class 3; record ice_grade "roughly AI1" is not sourced.

overview: A steep, rarely climbed line up Golden Horn's sheer north face, first climbed by Fred Beckey and Roe 'Duke' Watson in 1958; little is known of it beyond its first ascent.
beta: Catalogued as a distinct technical alpine route from the southwest standard route, but very little published trip-report detail exists — the north and east faces of Golden Horn are noted regionally as sheer and infrequently climbed.

first_pass.evidence: Only the 1958 Beckey-Watson FA is recorded; no grade published anywhere found.
first_pass.note: Left ungraded rather than invent a number; record has no grade columns either.

face: North ridge, from the deep notch just north of the summit fin
fa: Helmy Beckey, Fred Beckey, and Walt Varney, June 17, 1942 (first ascent of the peak)
overview: Half Moon is a crescent-shaped granite fin on the north half of Kangaroo Ridge, between Wallaby Peak and Big Kangaroo, about two miles east of the North Cascades Highway at Washington Pass. It has no easy way up: every line to its summit is a roped rock climb, and the easiest is fifth class. The North Ridge starts in the deep notch just north of the fin and climbs about seven pitches on or just west of the crest to the summit. The rock is friable and eroded on the first pitch or two and much bet
beta: Start in the deep notch north of the peak and climb the broad buttress above it toward the ridge crest. The first pitch has hollow, friable rock that improves steadily on the second. From there the line stays on the crest or just west of it, belaying at ledges, with steeper crack climbing in the middle of the route. High on the ridge a pitch traverses the west side of the narrowing crest with big exposure over the west face before working back to the crest. The last pitch is easy climbing on the
breakdown: Pitch 7 — summit crest: Easy 5th class, then scrambling

first_pass.evidence: Easiest route is 5th class; at least 3 routes, none easy; no number found for the North Ridge, kept the record 5.7.

fa: Ed Cooper, Glen Denny, Joan Firey, Joe Firey, George Whitmore — September 8, 1961 (also the peak's overall first ascent)
overview: Himmelhorn (originally Himmelgeisterhorn, "Horn of the Sky Spirit") is one of the most sought-after summits of the Southern Pickets, sitting on the crest between Ottohorn/Frenzel Spitz to the west and Twin Needles/Mount Terror to the east, with the small Mustard Glacier draped on its north side. It was first climbed September 8, 1961 by Ed Cooper, Glen Denny, Joan Firey, Joe Firey, and George Whitmore, who approached via the west notch (the Himmel-Otto col) and found a class 4 line up a ledge sy
beta: First ascensionists Cooper, Denny, and the Fireys found the peak unpromising from either flanking notch, then located a class-4 route by following a ledge onto the north face that wasn't visible from below. The line is mostly scrambling with short steeper steps; conditions and difficulty vary considerably with season and snow coverage in the approach gully.

first_pass.evidence: Beckey: mainly class 4 with one lead of moderate class 5; no number published.
first_pass.note: id says southeast_route but the standard route is on the northwest aspect (face column agrees with NW).

overview: One of the North Peak's easier class 3-4 scrambling lines, ascending the ridge toward the South Peak saddle.

first_pass.evidence: North Peak easiest routes rated class 4 snow/rock scramble; no source found for this South Ridge line specifically.

face: Northwest Buttress (northwest side, above the Home Creek basin)
overview: The original 1983 line up Inner Constance's northwest buttress; the 2021 route Sean's Route/Second Wind climbs a variation finish on this same buttress.
beta: Documentation of this line is sparse, and there is no full route description. Climbers who have scouted it describe very poor rock overall — near the summit ridge, as bad as any in the Olympics — with a possible band of somewhat better rock on the north side, but caution that any existing description should be taken 'with a grain of salt' and the line ground-truthed in person.

first_pass.evidence: No published grade for the 1983 original line was found; MP describes the shared upper buttress as class 4-low fifth, and the record's breakdown says 'Low 5th'.
first_pass.note: 'Low 5th' with no number anywhere, mapped to 5.0.

route: Standard Route (Northeast summit via South Gully and East Ridge)
face: South Gully and East Ridge, above Avalanche Canyon
fa: Unknown; first ascent of peak 1939 by David Harrah party
overview: Inner Constance (7,672 ft by LiDAR) is the fifth-highest summit in the Olympic Mountains, a rugged pyramid just west of Mount Constance (its line parent, 0.9 mi east) across the glacially carved Avalanche Canyon, within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park. The mountain is built of Eocene tilted pillow basalt, rotten and loose throughout. David Harrah's party is credited with the first ascent in 1939. The commonly described standard line climbs out of Avalanche Canyon via a So
beta: From Lake Constance, ascend Avalanche Canyon on climber paths and snow patches to a broad couloir below The Thumb landmark. Ascend the broad couloir on firm snow, veering right into a steeper secondary couloir. Follow a narrow, snow-filled defile on the right side, featuring a hard snow finger with moats. At higher elevations, climb a steep snow gully with discontinuous snow finger, stemming out to rock and scrambling up the moat. Gain the east ridge crest via a final pitch of Class 3 rock, then

first_pass.evidence: Trip report via the South Gully and East Ridge: a snow defile with moats, then a Class 2-3 scramble to the top; no 5th-class climbing mentioned. The record's own breakdown tops out at Class 3-4.
first_pass.note: The rock_grade 5.0 and the headline 'low 5th' are supported neither by any source found nor by the record's own breakdown; Class 4 is the top of its own Class 3-4 section.
